## Introduction

This page collects tips and tricks that will make you more efficient in VS Code.
None of this is required for the course,
but the time you invest in learning your editor will pay off quickly,
since you'll spend many hours in it.

Nearly everything here applies both to VS Code at OSC,
which runs in your browser,
and to a VS Code installation on your own computer.

::: {.callout-tip}
#### When a keyboard shortcut doesn't work
Because VS Code at OSC runs inside your browser,
a few keyboard shortcuts are "captured" by the browser instead of by VS Code.
For example, <kbd>Ctrl/⌘</kbd>+<kbd>W</kbd> may close your _browser tab_
rather than the file you have open in the editor.

Whenever a shortcut doesn't do what you expect,
you can find the same functionality through the menus
or the Command Palette ([see below](#the-command-palette)).
:::

## Finding functionality

### The Command Palette

To find and apply any menu option that is available in VS Code,
the so-called "Command Palette" is handy.
To access it, click {{< fa cog >}} and then `Command Palette`
(or press <kbd>F1</kbd> or <kbd>Ctrl/⌘</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>P</kbd>).
To use it, start typing something to search for an option.

The Command Palette also shows the keyboard shortcut for each option, if there is one,
so it is a good way to discover shortcuts for things you do often.

### Keyboard shortcuts overview

For a single-page PDF overview of keyboard shortcuts for your operating system:
{{< fa bars >}}   \>   `Help`   \>   `Keyboard Shortcut Reference`.
(Or for direct links to these PDFs on the web:
[Windows](https://code.visualstudio.com/shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-windows.pdf){target="_blank"} /
[Mac](https://code.visualstudio.com/shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-macos.pdf){target="_blank"} /
[Linux](https://code.visualstudio.com/shortcuts/keyboard-shortcuts-linux.pdf){target="_blank"}.)

To see, change, or add keyboard shortcuts,
click {{< fa cog >}} > `Keyboard Shortcuts`,
like you did in class to add the <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Enter</kbd> shortcut
to send code to the terminal.

## Working in the editor

### Line actions

- **Automatic whole-line selection**\
  In VS Code's editor pane,
  the _entire line that your cursor is on is selected by default_.
  As such, you don't need to manually select the entire line when wanting to send
  it to the terminal --- or when cutting/copying lines!
  The standard copy and cut shortcuts
  (<kbd>Ctrl/⌘</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> / <kbd>X</kbd>)
  will **cut/copy the entire line** that the cursor is on.

- **Move a line up or down**: <kbd>Alt/Option</kbd>+<kbd>⬆</kbd>/<kbd>⬇</kbd>

- **Delete a line**: <kbd>Ctrl/⌘</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>K</kbd>

- **Comment or uncomment a line**: <kbd>Ctrl/⌘</kbd>+<kbd>/</kbd>\
  This inserts or removes the comment character for the current language,
  e.g. `#` in a shell script.
  This is handy to temporarily deactivate ("comment out") code.

All of the above also work for **multiple selected lines at once**.

### Go to a specific line

Error messages often mention a line number, as in:

```bash-out-solo
scripts/fastqc.sh: line 8: $1: unbound variable
```

To jump to a line, press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>G</kbd> (on a Mac too)
and type the line number.
Alternatively, click on the `Ln <number>, Col <number>` indicator
in the Status Bar at the bottom of the window.

### Find and replace

- **Find** in the current file: <kbd>Ctrl/⌘</kbd>+<kbd>F</kbd>.
- **Find and replace** in the current file:
  <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>H</kbd> (Windows/Linux) or
  <kbd>Option</kbd>+<kbd>⌘</kbd>+<kbd>F</kbd> (Mac).
- **Search across all files** in the folder you opened in VS Code:
  click the magnifying glass icon in the Activity Bar,
  or press <kbd>Ctrl/⌘</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>F</kbd>.
  You can also replace across files from there.

The search box has buttons to make your search case-sensitive (`Aa`),
match whole words only (`ab`), or use a regular expression (`.*`).

### Multiple cursors

VS Code lets you type in multiple places at once,
which is great for making the same edit on several lines:

- **Add a cursor** where you click: hold <kbd>Alt/Option</kbd> while clicking.
- **Select the next occurrence** of the currently selected text:
  <kbd>Ctrl/⌘</kbd>+<kbd>D</kbd> (press repeatedly to add more occurrences).
- **Column ("box") selection**: hold <kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>Alt/Option</kbd>
  while dragging your mouse.

Press <kbd>Esc</kbd> to go back to a single cursor.

## Navigating files and panes

### Quick Open

To open a file without clicking through the Explorer,
press <kbd>Ctrl/⌘</kbd>+<kbd>P</kbd> and start typing (part of) its name.

### The Explorer

- **Copying a file's path**\
  Right-click on a file in the Explorer and select `Copy Path` (absolute path)
  or `Copy Relative Path` (relative to the folder you opened in VS Code).
  This is handy for pasting file paths into the terminal or into a script.

- **Moving files**\
  You can drag and drop files and folders in the Explorer to move them.

- **Downloading files**\
  Right-click on any file,
  and among the options shown, you should see "**Download...**".
  Click on that to download the file to your computer!
  There is no way to upload, though --- this should be done through the OnDemand
  file browser
  (or using a terminal on your own computer; you'll learn more about that later).

### Arranging your screen

- **Toggling (hiding/showing) the side bars**\
  If you want to save some screen space while coding along in class,
  you may want to occasionally hide the side bars:
  - In {{< fa bars >}} > `View` > `Appearance`,
    you can toggle both the `Activity Bar` and the `Primary Side Bar`.
  - For the primary/wide side bar, you can also drag it away,
    or use the keyboard shortcut <kbd>Ctrl/⌘</kbd>+<kbd>B</kbd>.

- **Splitting the editor**\
  To see two files side by side (e.g., a script and your `README.md`),
  drag an editor tab to the right side of the editor pane,
  or right-click on a tab and select `Split Right`.

- **Switching between the terminal and the editor**
  - Open a terminal, or move from the editor to the terminal:
    <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>\`</kbd> (backtick)
  - Move from the terminal to the editor: <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>1</kbd>

### Multiple terminals

You can have multiple terminals open at once ---
for example, to run a long command in one while you keep working in another.
In the Terminal pane:

- Click the `+` icon to open a new terminal.
- Switch between terminals in the list on the right side of the pane.
- Click the trash can icon to close ("kill") a terminal.

Keep in mind that each terminal is a separate shell session:
variables you assign and modules you load in one terminal
are not available in the other.

## Settings

You can open the Settings via {{< fa cog >}} > `Settings`,
and then search for the setting you want to change.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### User settings vs. workspace settings _(Click to expand)_

The Settings editor has two tabs at the top: `User` and `Workspace`.

- **User** settings apply everywhere you use VS Code.
- **Workspace** settings only apply to the folder you currently have open,
  and are saved in a file `.vscode/settings.json` inside that folder.

Change your User settings unless you have a specific reason to do otherwise.
:::

Some settings you may want to change:

- **Auto Save**\
  Auto-saving is turned on by default using the "afterDelay" option. You can:
  - Quickly turn it off by clicking {{< fa bars >}} > `File` > `Auto Save`
    (shows a checkmark when activated).
  - Search for "Auto Save" in the Settings, where you can pick from several options.

- **Word wrap**\
  By default, long lines run off the right side of the editor.
  To wrap them instead, click {{< fa bars >}} > `View` > `Word Wrap`
  (or press <kbd>Alt/Option</kbd>+<kbd>Z</kbd>).
  To make this permanent, search for "Word Wrap" in the Settings.

- **Minimap**\
  The "minimap" is the zoomed-out view of your file on the right side of the editor.
  If you find it distracting, you can hide it via
  {{< fa bars >}} > `View` > `Appearance` > `Minimap`.

- **Font size**\
  Search for "Font Size" in the Settings to change the font size
  of the editor ("Editor: Font Size")
  and, separately, of the terminal ("Terminal › Integrated: Font Size").

- **A vertical line to mark line length**\
  To keep your lines of code and Markdown text from getting too long,
  you can show one or more vertical lines ("rulers") at a specific width:
  search for "Rulers" in the Settings, click `Edit in settings.json`,
  and add e.g. `80` between the square brackets: `"editor.rulers": [80]`.

- **Tidying up whitespace**\
  Search for and turn on "Trim Trailing Whitespace"
  (removes spaces at the ends of lines when you save a file) and
  "Insert Final Newline" (makes sure a file ends with a newline,
  which some command-line tools expect).

## Extensions

VS Code extensions are small programs that add functionality to VS Code.
To install one, click the Extensions icon in the Activity Bar (see screenshot below),
search for the extension, and click `Install`.

![](/img/vscode-extension-icon.png){fig-align="center" width="8%" fig-alt="The VS Code Extensions icon." .lightbox}

::: legend2
Activity Bar, with the Extensions icon (bottom) highlighted.
:::

### Extensions used in the course

- **HTML Preview** (by *Thomas Haakon Townsend*) ---
  view HTML files, like FastQC output, inside VS Code _(week 6)_.
- **ShellCheck** (by *timonwong*) --- check your shell scripts for errors
  and bad practices _(week 7)_.
  At OSC, this needs a work-around to function ---
  see the [first shell scripting lecture](../week07/w7a_scripts.qmd#install-shellcheck).

### Other useful extensions

- **Rainbow CSV** (by *mechatroner*) ---
  makes CSV/TSV files easier to view in the editor pane,
  with column-based colors.
- **Code Spell Checker** (by *Street Side Software*) ---
  flags spelling mistakes in your Markdown files and code comments.
- **markdownlint** (by *David Anson*) ---
  checks your Markdown files for formatting issues and inconsistencies.
- **Markdown All in One** (by *Yu Zhang*) ---
  adds keyboard shortcuts for Markdown formatting,
  automatic list continuation, and table of contents generation.
